author: Stone Fox Capital
title: Apple: Ignored Truth - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
The market has spent the last month since Apple ( AAPL ) announced the intent to shift away from reporting iPhone units fretting over the implications on demand. What the market is ignoring is the truth about the Services future of the tech giant. Down at $180, the stock is far too cheap for the higher margins of the recurring revenue stream future.
Image Source: Apple website
Services-Led Opportunity Katy Huberty of Morgan Stanley predicts that Apple will reach Services revenues of $100 billion by 2023 ( via Appleinsider ). As an example, the tech giant just topped quarterly Services revenues of $10 billion for an annual run rate of $40 billion.
Markets love this type of consistent growth. Morgan Stanley predicts a stock price of $253 based on sustainable Services growth in the 20% range. Apple reported 27% growth in FQ4 and ended FY18 with related revenues of $37.2 billion. Based on the 20% growth rate, annual revenues would come out to the following amounts (note that growth in the next couple of years should approach 25% to reach her $100 billion target):
FY18A - $37.2B FY19E - $44.6B FY20E - $53.6B FY21E - $64.3B FY22E - $77.2B FY23E - $92.6B The analyst prediction is based on Apple users increasing spending on additional Services from $120 annually to $220 by FY23 from an increased penetration of Cloud, Care and Music, among others. The key here is that iPhone units sold in FY19 aren't as meaningful as the amount in service. The number of active iPhone users was estimated at 700 million last year and should soon top 1 billion.
The biggest issue is that the iPhone still accounts for the vast majority of revenues. In FQ4, Services reached a record at $9.98 billion, but the amount was dwarfed by iPhone sales at $37.2 billion. Even combined iPad and Mac sales at $11.5 billion topped those of the Services.
The key in the last year is that the gap wasn't closing due to the growth of the iPhone. In FQ4, iPhone revenues surged by 29% and actually topped the adjusted 27% growth of the Services group. Going forward, Services expects to keep 20%-plus growth in place while most analysts now expect iPhone sales to potentially dip.
Total revenues hit $265 billion last fiscal year and analysts on average still forecast growth this year. The main growth driver will be Services where 25% growth in FY19 would add $9.3 billion in revenues. Increasingly, Services will provide a $10 billion annual growth driver of high-margin revenues to offset any weakness in iPhone sales.
Services-Led Margin Inflection A lot of the tech giants have recently hit margin inflection points due to the shifts to recurring revenues. My last article discussed the inflection point at Amazon ( AMZN ) as the company started breaking out AWS revenues. Microsoft ( MSFT ) hit a similar inflection point in 2016 as gross margins bottomed out as the stock was around $50.
MSFT data by YCharts Interestingly, Microsoft recently passed Apple for the most valuable company. The stocks are neck and neck right now around a market cap of $820 billion due largely to the larger multiple obtained by Microsoft.
AAPL PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts A lot of investors have been disappointed that Apple hasn't seen any margin lift from the recent growth in Services, especially since the company confirmed the group has higher margins. Katy Huberty places the average gross margin of the division at above 50% with devices at 35%. The total gross margins over the last decade has constantly shifted down toward 38%, from around 42% in 2013.
AAPL Gross Profit Margin (TTM) data by YCharts The issue is likely two fold in that the shift to Music is likely hampering the growth in the Services margins and the massive growth in the iPhone and even the Watch recently have obscured the benefit of the higher margins from Services. Note that Google search and App Store revenues are very high margin while Music probably has similar gross margins as Spotify ( SPOT ) that's down in the mid-20% range.
Huberty forecasts that Apple Music revenues will surge from $4 billion in FY18 to $13.7 billion in FY23. The key is the likely very low margin Apple Music will count for less than 15% of forecasted Services revenues in FY23.
Since Apple doesn't provide actual margins per product, the market has to constantly guess on actual numbers. Using a 35% gross margin for Products and 56% for Services roughly matches the correct gross margin in the last quarter and year. The below table shows the gross margins over the next three fiscal years using the above gross margins and flat Product revenue with Services growing by 25% annually.
Under such a scenario, gross margins grow from 38% in FY18 to over 40% in FY21. Under such a scenario, gross profits double to over $40 billion in the three years without any revenue growth from Products where the Watch is sure to offset any iPhone weakness.
Ultimately, Products will probably grow as well with initial success in wearables and the long-term shift toward higher ASP iPhones. The goal of this exercise is to show the ability of gross profits to surge from the high-margin Services division alone. Revenues from Products just need to flat line and gross margins will jump.
Takeaway The key investor takeaway is that other tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft soared as margins expanded over the last few years. Apple is poised to follow the same trajectory making the stock a bargain at $180 and trading for about 12.2x forward EPS estimates while Microsoft trades at a 22x forward multiple. The market is ignoring the truth about the Services division.
